checkpoints: `ensureTranscoded` guards against re-running the encode with a single check — whether `manifest.m3u8` already exists on disk — and nothing else; there is no lock or claim placed on a `videoId` before the ladder starts.

Because the existence check and the encode work are not atomic, every concurrent request for the same cold video (a `POST encode` call and several first `manifest.m3u8` fetches arriving together) sees the file missing at the same instant and independently starts the full three-rung FFmpeg ladder, multiplying CPU by the number of simultaneous requests instead of costing one ladder per video.

With no in-flight lock, these parallel ladders also race to write the same output files (segments and the master playlist), so whichever run finishes last wins and the others' encoding work is wasted or can corrupt the result.

The fix is coalescing concurrent callers onto a single run rather than adding a bigger lock around the whole method: keep an in-flight `Map<string, Promise<void>>` on the service, and once the existence check misses, look the `videoId` up in that map before starting any work.

If a promise for that `videoId` is already in the map, the caller awaits it and returns instead of starting a second run; if not, the caller starts the encode, stores its promise in the map synchronously before the first `await` so a concurrent caller sees it immediately, and removes the entry in a `finally` once the run settles.
This coalescing pattern is the same shape as request-deduping or dataloader batching, just keyed by `videoId` — it turns N concurrent first-requests for a cold video into exactly one FFmpeg run.

An in-memory map only protects a single process; if encoding must be durable across multiple server instances, `ensureTranscoded` needs to move onto a job queue (e.g. BullMQ) keyed by `videoId`, so a second instance also awaits the existing job instead of starting its own.

Lazy transcoding is the right default for a library where most uploads are never watched, since it avoids spending CPU on clips nobody opens, but it forces the first viewer of any video to wait out the full ladder before their manifest resolves.
Eager pre-encoding on upload makes the first play instant because the ladder already ran, but it burns CPU and storage transcoding effectively all uploads, most of which are never watched.

A reasonable middle ground is to eager-encode only content with an existing signal of being hot (an established creator, a flagged launch) and keep the lock-protected lazy path as the fallback for the long tail of uploads.

The metric that proves the coalescing fix worked is the count of concurrent FFmpeg processes, or `ensureTranscoded` calls that actually reach the encode loop rather than hitting the map and awaiting, per cold `videoId` — this scales with request concurrency before the fix and is pinned at exactly 1 after it.

A test that fires many concurrent `POST encode` calls for one fresh video id and asserts exactly one FFmpeg run occurred, producing one clean (non-corrupted) manifest, demonstrates the fix rather than just plausibly describing it.
